topics.title: Elements of Criminal Liability
topics.content:
Every offence under the Penal Code (Act 574) requires proof of two essential elements:

**1. Actus Reus (Guilty Act)**
The physical element: conduct, omission, consequence, or state of affairs prohibited by law. Section 33 defines 'act' to include a series of acts, and 'omission' to include a series of omissions.

**2. Mens Rea (Guilty Mind)**
The mental element: intention (niat), knowledge (pengetahuan), recklessness, or negligence. The Penal Code does not use 'mens rea' as a term but uses words like 'intentionally', 'knowingly', 'fraudulently', 'dishonestly', 'voluntarily' (Section 39), 'rashly', and 'negligently'.

**Concurrence Principle**
Both elements must coexist at the same time. See *Fagan v Metropolitan Police Commissioner* [1969] 1 QB 439 (applied locally).

**Burden of Proof**
The prosecution bears the legal burden of proving both elements beyond reasonable doubt (Section 101 Evidence Act 1950 read with *Mat v PP* [1963] MLJ 263).
topics.description: Actus reus and mens rea — the two pillars of criminal liability under Malaysian law.

topics.title: Classification of Offences
topics.content:
**By Power of Arrest (First Schedule, CPC):**
- *Seizable* (boleh tangkap): police may arrest without warrant.
- *Non-seizable* (tak boleh tangkap): warrant required.

**By Right to Bail:**
- *Bailable*: accused has a right to bail (Section 387 CPC).
- *Non-bailable*: bail at court's discretion (Section 388 CPC).

**By Mode of Trial:**
- *Summary*: tried by Magistrate.
- *Triable in Sessions Court*: punishable with up to 20 years imprisonment.
- *Exclusive High Court jurisdiction*: offences punishable by death (e.g., murder, drug trafficking).

**By Compoundability:**
- *Compoundable* (Section 260 CPC, Sixth Schedule): may be settled.
- *Non-compoundable*: cannot be withdrawn by complainant alone.
topics.description: Seizable/non-seizable, bailable/non-bailable, summary/indictable.

topics.title: Strict Liability Offences
topics.content:
Although the general rule requires mens rea, some statutes create strict liability offences where mens rea is excluded.

**Test (Lim Chin Aik v R [1963] AC 160):**
1. Is the offence regulatory (public welfare) in nature?
2. Would imposing strict liability promote enforcement?
3. Is mens rea capable of being read into the statute?

**Examples in Malaysia:**
- Many provisions of the Road Transport Act 1987.
- Customs Act 1967.
- Environmental Quality Act 1974.
- Some Food Act 1983 offences.

**Defences still available:**
- Honest and reasonable mistake of fact (limited).
- Statutory defences specifically provided.
topics.description: Offences not requiring proof of mens rea.

topics.title: Common Intention (Section 34 Penal Code)
topics.content:
**Section 34**: 'When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each of such persons is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone.'

**Essential ingredients:**
1. Criminal act done by several persons.
2. Common intention to commit that act.
3. Participation in the criminal act.
4. Pre-arranged plan.

**Key cases:**
- *Mahbub Shah v Emperor* AIR 1945 PC 118 — common intention must be pre-arranged.
- *Namasiyiam v PP* [1987] 2 MLJ 336 — common intention may develop on the spot.
- *PP v Yeo Choon Poh* [1994] 2 MLJ 541.

**Distinction from Section 149** (common object — unlawful assembly): Section 34 requires participation, Section 149 imputes liability by mere membership.
topics.description: Joint criminal liability where act done in furtherance of common intention.

topics.title: Abetment (Sections 107-120 Penal Code)
topics.content:
**Section 107** defines abetment in three ways:
1. **Instigation** — actively suggesting, urging, or provoking another.
2. **Conspiracy** — engaging in conspiracy where an act/omission takes place pursuant to it.
3. **Aiding** — intentionally facilitating the offence by act or illegal omission.

**Punishment (Section 109)**: Same as principal offence if act abetted is committed.
**Section 116**: Punishment if offence not committed.

**Key principles:**
- The abettor must have knowledge of the principal offender's criminal intent.
- Mere presence is not abetment unless presence itself encourages the offence.
- *PP v Datuk Tan Cheng Swee* [1980] 2 MLJ 277 — mens rea of abetment.
- *Sabarudin Non v PP* [2005] 4 MLJ 37.
topics.description: Liability for instigating, conspiring, or aiding the commission of an offence.

topics.title: Criminal Conspiracy (Sections 120A-120B)
topics.content:
**Section 120A**: Criminal conspiracy is an agreement by two or more persons to do (or cause to be done) an illegal act, or a legal act by illegal means.

**Essential elements:**
1. Agreement (express or implied).
2. Two or more persons.
3. Object: illegal act, or legal act by illegal means.
4. For non-offence conspiracies, an overt act in pursuance is required.

**Punishment (Section 120B):**
- Conspiracy to commit offence punishable with death/life/2+ years imprisonment: same as abetment.
- Other conspiracies: up to 6 months imprisonment or fine.

**Cases:**
- *PP v Yuvaraj* [1969] 2 MLJ 89 (PC).
- *Yong Vui Kong v PP* [2010] 3 MLJ 489.
topics.description: Agreement between two or more persons to commit illegal act.

topics.title: Attempt (Sections 511 & specific provisions)
topics.content:
**Section 511** is the general attempt provision: punishment is up to half of the longest term provided for the offence (or full fine).

**Specific attempt provisions:**
- Section 307: Attempt to murder.
- Section 308: Attempt to commit culpable homicide.
- Section 309: Attempt to commit suicide (now repealed in many jurisdictions).
- Section 393: Attempt to commit robbery.

**Test for attempt:**
1. Mens rea: intention to commit the substantive offence.
2. Actus reus: act sufficiently proximate to commission (more than mere preparation).

**Key authorities:**
- *R v Eagleton* (1855) — last act test.
- *Munah binti Ali v PP* [1958] MLJ 159.
- *PP v Yong Heng Yew* [1996] 3 MLJ 66.
topics.description: Liability for attempted offences under Malaysian criminal law.

topics.title: General Exceptions (Chapter IV Penal Code)
topics.content:
**Sections 76-106** contain general exceptions:

- **S.76**: Act done by person bound by law.
- **S.79**: Act done by person justified or believing himself justified by law.
- **S.80**: Accident in doing a lawful act.
- **S.81**: Act likely to cause harm done without criminal intent to prevent other harm (necessity).
- **S.82-83**: Act of a child under 10/under 12 with insufficient understanding (doli incapax).
- **S.84**: Act of person of unsound mind (insanity / McNaughten Rules).
- **S.85-86**: Intoxication.
- **S.87-93**: Consent.
- **S.94**: Act done under duress (threats).
- **S.96-106**: Private defence of body and property.

**Burden**: Once accused raises defence, burden shifts to prosecution to disprove beyond reasonable doubt (subject to Section 105 Evidence Act 1950 for some defences).
topics.description: Statutory defences: mistake, accident, necessity, infancy, insanity, intoxication, consent, private defence.

topics.title: Article 5 — Liberty of the Person
topics.content:
**Article 5(1)**: No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty save in accordance with law.

**Article 5(2)**: Where complaint is made of unlawful detention, the High Court shall inquire and order release if not lawful.

**Article 5(3)**: When arrested, the person:
- Shall be informed of grounds of arrest as soon as may be.
- Shall be allowed to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of his choice.

**Article 5(4)**: Must be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours.

**Article 5(5)**: Clauses 3 and 4 do not apply to enemy aliens.

**Cases:**
- *Ooi Ah Phua v OCCI Kedah* [1975] 2 MLJ 198.
- *Saul Hamid v PP* [1987] 2 MLJ 736.
- *Lee Mau Seng v Minister of Home Affairs* [1971] 2 MLJ 137.
- *Hashim bin Saud v Yahaya bin Hashim* [1977] 2 MLJ 116.
topics.description: Constitutional safeguards on arrest, detention, and right to counsel.

topics.title: Article 7 — Protection Against Retrospective Criminal Laws
topics.content:
**Article 7(1)**: No person shall be punished for an act or omission which was not punishable by law when it was done or made; nor shall any person suffer greater punishment than was prescribed by law at the time it was committed.

**Article 7(2)**: A person who has been acquitted or convicted of an offence shall not be tried again for the same offence (autrefois acquit / autrefois convict) — except on order of a superior court for retrial.

**Statutory equivalent**: Section 302 CPC.

**Cases:**
- *PP v Mohamed Ismail* [1984] 2 MLJ 219.
- *Jamali bin Adnan v PP* [1986] 1 MLJ 162.
topics.description: Prohibition on ex post facto criminalisation and double jeopardy.

topics.title: Article 8 — Equality Before the Law
topics.content:
Article 8 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the law. It also prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, descent, place of birth, or gender.

**Application in criminal law:**
- Selective prosecution may be challenged.
- Sentencing parity for similarly situated offenders.
- Equal access to bail and legal representation.

**Cases:**
- *Beatrice Fernandez v Sistem Penerbangan Malaysia* [2005] 3 MLJ 681.
- *Datuk Haji Harun v PP* [1977] 2 MLJ 155.
- *PP v Khong Teng Khen* [1976] 2 MLJ 166.
topics.description: Equal protection in criminal proceedings.

topics.title: Right to Fair Trial
topics.content:
Although not expressly enumerated, the right to a fair trial is implied in Article 5(1) ('save in accordance with law').

**Components:**
1. Independent and impartial tribunal.
2. Presumption of innocence.
3. Right to be informed of the charge.
4. Right to adequate time and facilities to prepare defence.
5. Right to legal representation.
6. Right to examine prosecution witnesses (Article 5(3) and Section 138 EA).
7. Right to call defence witnesses.
8. Right to interpreter (Section 270 CPC).
9. Right against self-incrimination (Section 132 EA).
10. Right to public trial (subject to exceptions).

**Key authority**: *Lee Kwan Woh v PP* [2009] 5 MLJ 301 — Article 5(1) read together with Article 8(1) gives birth to the doctrine of substantive due process.
topics.description: Components of fair trial under Article 5 and natural justice.

topics.title: Powers of Arrest (CPC Chapter V)
topics.content:
**Without warrant (Section 23 CPC)** — police may arrest:
- Person concerned in seizable offence.
- Person possessing housebreaking implements.
- Person possessing suspected stolen property.
- Person obstructing police officer.
- Escapee, deserter, etc.

**With warrant (Sections 38–46 CPC)**: Court issues warrant directed to police; valid throughout Malaysia.

**By private person (Section 27 CPC)**: May arrest any person committing seizable offence in their view; must hand over to police without unnecessary delay.

**By Magistrate (Section 30 CPC)**: May arrest any person committing offence in his presence within his local jurisdiction.

**Mode of arrest (Section 15 CPC)**: Touch or confine the body, unless submission to custody by word/action. Use only as much force as necessary.
topics.description: Arrest with and without warrant — Sections 15–34 CPC.

topics.title: Search and Seizure
topics.content:
**Search of arrested person (Section 20 CPC)**: Police may search and place any articles found in safe custody.

**Search of place (Sections 51–62 CPC)**:
- Section 51: Court may issue summons for production of documents.
- Section 54: Search warrant may be issued.
- Section 56: Search without warrant in certain situations (after arrest, urgent).
- Section 62: Search of persons in or about a place searched.

**Special search powers**:
- Section 116(1): Search by police during investigation.
- Section 23 DDA 1952: Search for dangerous drugs.
- MACC Act 2009 — special search powers.

**Procedural safeguards**:
- Two reputable witnesses (Section 60 CPC).
- List of seized items (Section 64 CPC).
- Search must generally be in presence of occupant.
topics.description: Search of persons, premises, and seizure of evidence under the CPC.

topics.title: Police Investigation (Section 107–120 CPC)
topics.content:
**First Information Report (Section 107 CPC)**: Information relating to commission of seizable offence given to police orally or in writing; reduced to writing and read over.

**Investigation steps**:
- Section 110: Examination of witnesses by police; statements recorded but not signed.
- Section 111: No threats, inducements, or promises.
- Section 112: Police investigation diary.
- Section 113: Admissibility of accused's statements (cautioned statement).

**Remand (Section 117 CPC)**:
- First production: up to 4 days for offences punishable up to 14 years.
- Up to 7 days for offences punishable above 14 years or capital offences.
- Magistrate must record reasons; cannot exceed 15 days in total.

**Refer**: *Re Detention of Sivarasa Rasiah* [1996] 3 MLJ 611.
topics.description: Information of offences, investigation procedure, and remand.

topics.title: Bail and Bond (Sections 387–400 CPC)
topics.content:
**Bailable offences (Section 387)**: Accused has right to bail; police or court must release.

**Non-bailable offences (Section 388)**: Bail at court's discretion. Court considers:
- Nature and seriousness of offence.
- Strength of evidence.
- Likelihood of absconding.
- Risk of interference with witnesses.
- Health, age, antecedents of accused.

**Unbailable offences**: Where statute expressly prohibits bail (e.g., Section 39B DDA before recent amendments).

**Capital offences**: Bail very rarely granted; *PP v Dato' Mat* [1991] 2 MLJ 186.

**Special bail provisions**:
- Section 388A: Bail may be granted with conditions (reporting, surrender of passport).
- Section 389: Amount of bail not excessive.
- Section 390: Sureties.
- Section 397: Forfeiture of bond.
- Section 311 CPC: Bail pending appeal.
topics.description: Bailable, non-bailable, and unbailable offences; conditions and forfeiture.

topics.title: Charge and Joinder (Sections 152–172 CPC)
topics.content:
**Section 152 CPC**: Every charge shall state the offence with which the accused is charged.
**Section 153**: Where the law gives the offence a specific name, the offence may be described in the charge by that name only.
**Section 154**: The law and section under which the offence is punishable shall be mentioned.
**Section 156**: Particulars as to time and place; thing in respect of which offence committed.
**Section 158**: Charge shall be in the language of the court.

**Joinder rules**:
- Section 163: Three offences of same kind within 12 months may be joined.
- Section 164: Offences forming same transaction.
- Section 165: Where doubt exists which offence committed.
- Section 170: Joint trial of multiple accused for same offence.

**Defective charge**: Section 422 — no error in charge shall be material unless it occasioned a failure of justice.
topics.description: Form of charge, particulars, joinder of charges and accused.

topics.title: Plea and Plea Bargaining (Sections 172A–172H CPC)
topics.content:
**Plea taking**: Charge read and explained in language understood by accused; accused asked to plead.

**Guilty plea (Section 173(b))** — court must:
1. Be satisfied accused understands nature and consequences.
2. Record plea in accused's own words if possible.
3. Convict only if facts disclose offence.
4. Hear mitigation before sentence.

**Plea bargaining (Sections 172A–172H, introduced 2010)**:
- Section 172C: Application by accused before commencement of trial.
- Section 172D: Court may invite parties to negotiate.
- Section 172E: Bargain may relate to charge or sentence.
- Section 172F: Court may accept or reject plea bargain.
- Where bargain accepted, sentence shall not be less than half the minimum and not more than half the maximum.

**Cases**: *PP v Hanif Basree Abdul Rahman* [2008] 4 MLJ 514.
topics.description: Guilty plea, claiming trial, and plea bargaining procedure.

topics.title: Criminal Trial Procedure (Sections 173–183 CPC)
topics.content:
**Order of trial**:
1. Accused brought before court; charge read.
2. Plea taken; if not guilty, trial proceeds.
3. Prosecution opens case (optional).
4. Prosecution calls witnesses; defence cross-examines.
5. At close of prosecution case, court determines prima facie case (Section 173(f) / 180).
6. If prima facie case made out, accused called upon to enter defence; choices:
   (a) Give sworn evidence.
   (b) Make unsworn statement from dock.
   (c) Remain silent.
7. Defence calls witnesses; prosecution cross-examines.
8. Closing submissions.
9. Judgment.

**Prima facie test (Balachandran v PP [2005] 2 MLJ 301)**: Maximum evaluation of prosecution evidence; credible evidence proving each ingredient of offence.
topics.description: Order of trial, prima facie case, defence, judgment.

topics.title: Judgment, Sentencing, and Appeal
topics.content:
**Judgment (Section 307 CPC)**: Pronounced in open court; reasons recorded.

**Sentencing principles (PP v Loo Choon Fatt [1976] 2 MLJ 256)**:
1. Retribution / punishment.
2. Deterrence (general and specific).
3. Prevention.
4. Rehabilitation.

**Mitigation factors**: First offender, guilty plea, cooperation, restitution, age, family, remorse.
**Aggravating factors**: Premeditation, breach of trust, vulnerable victim, prevalence of offence.

**Appeal (Sections 305–323 CPC)**:
- Notice of Appeal: 14 days from decision.
- Petition of Appeal: 14 days from receipt of grounds of judgment.
- Magistrate → High Court → Court of Appeal → Federal Court (with leave).

**Revision (Section 323 CPC)**: High Court may revise any proceeding of Subordinate Court.
topics.description: Pronouncement of judgment, sentencing principles, and appellate procedure.

topics.title: Murder (Section 300 Penal Code)
topics.content:
**Section 300** — Culpable homicide is murder if:
(a) Done with intention of causing death.
(b) Done with intention of causing such bodily injury as the offender knows likely to cause death.
(c) Done with intention of causing bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
(d) Done with knowledge that act is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death.

**Exceptions** (reduce to culpable homicide not amounting to murder):
1. Grave and sudden provocation.
2. Exceeding right of private defence.
3. Public servant exceeding powers in good faith.
4. Sudden fight in heat of passion.
5. Consent (death of person above 18, with consent).

**Punishment (Section 302)**: Death, OR after 2018 amendments — imprisonment of not less than 30 years and not more than 40 years, AND whipping not less than 12 strokes.

**Cases**: *PP v Visuvanathan* [1977] 1 MLJ 178; *Tham Kai Yau v PP* [1977] 1 MLJ 174.
topics.description: Definition, ingredients, and exceptions to murder.

topics.title: Culpable Homicide (Sections 299, 304)
topics.content:
**Section 299**: Whoever causes death by doing an act:
- with intention of causing death; OR
- with intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death; OR
- with knowledge that he is likely by such act to cause death,
commits culpable homicide.

**Distinction from murder**: Murder is an aggravated form of culpable homicide. Section 299 = the genus; Section 300 = the species (murder).

**Section 304 — Punishment**:
(a) If act done with intention of causing death or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death — imprisonment up to 30 years AND fine.
(b) If done with knowledge that it is likely to cause death but without intention — imprisonment up to 10 years OR fine OR both.

**Cases**: *Tan Cheow Bock v PP* [1991] 3 MLJ 404; *Mohd Yatim v PP* [1950] MLJ 57.
topics.description: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

topics.title: Causing Hurt and Grievous Hurt
topics.content:
**Hurt (Section 319)**: Bodily pain, disease, or infirmity caused to any person.
**Voluntarily causing hurt (Section 321)**: Punishable up to 1 year imprisonment or RM2,000 fine or both (Section 323).

**Grievous hurt (Section 320)** — eight categories:
1. Emasculation.
2. Permanent privation of sight of either eye.
3. Permanent privation of hearing of either ear.
4. Privation of any member or joint.
5. Destruction or permanent impairing of powers of any member or joint.
6. Permanent disfiguration of head or face.
7. Fracture or dislocation of bone.
8. Hurt endangering life or causing severe bodily pain for 20+ days, or unable to follow ordinary pursuits.

**Section 325**: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt — up to 7 years imprisonment AND fine.
**Section 326**: With dangerous weapons — up to 20 years AND fine AND whipping.
**Section 326A**: Causing hurt to spouse — up to 10 years AND fine.
**Section 326B**: Acid attacks — life imprisonment AND whipping.
topics.description: Sections 319–338 Penal Code.

topics.title: Theft (Section 378 Penal Code)
topics.content:
**Section 378**: Whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moves that property in order to such taking, is said to commit theft.

**Five essential ingredients**:
1. Dishonest intention.
2. Property must be movable.
3. Property must be in possession of another.
4. Without consent.
5. Some movement of the property.

**Punishment (Section 379)**: Up to 7 years imprisonment OR fine OR both.

**Aggravated theft**:
- Section 379A: Theft of motor vehicle — minimum 1 year, up to 7 years AND fine.
- Section 380: Theft in dwelling house — up to 10 years AND fine.
- Section 381: Theft by clerk/servant — up to 10 years AND fine.
- Section 382: Theft after preparation for hurt/restraint — up to 10 years AND fine.

**Cases**: *PP v Tan Cheng Kwee* [1985] 2 MLJ 322; *Pyare Lal v State of Rajasthan* AIR 1963 SC 1094.
topics.description: Definition, essential ingredients, and aggravated forms.

topics.title: Robbery and Gang-Robbery
topics.content:
**Section 390 — Robbery**: Theft is robbery if, in committing theft, the offender voluntarily causes or attempts to cause:
- Death, hurt, or wrongful restraint, OR
- Fear of instant death, instant hurt, or instant wrongful restraint.

Extortion is robbery if offender, at time of extortion, is in presence of victim and puts him in fear of instant harm.

**Section 392 — Punishment**: Imprisonment 5–20 years AND whipping not less than 12 strokes; if on highway after sunset and before sunrise — 7–14 years.

**Section 394**: Voluntarily causing hurt during robbery — minimum 7 years.
**Section 397**: Robbery with deadly weapon or attempt to cause grievous hurt — minimum 7 years AND whipping not less than 12 strokes.

**Section 391 — Gang-robbery**: When five or more persons conjointly commit or attempt robbery.
**Section 395**: Punishment for gang-robbery — 20 years up to life AND whipping.
**Section 396**: Gang-robbery with murder — death or imprisonment for life AND whipping.
topics.description: Sections 390–402 Penal Code.

topics.title: Criminal Breach of Trust (Sections 405–409)
topics.content:
**Section 405**: Whoever, being in any manner entrusted with property, or with any dominion over property, dishonestly misappropriates or converts to his own use that property, or dishonestly uses or disposes of that property in violation of any direction of law or contract — commits CBT.

**Ingredients**:
1. Entrustment of property or dominion over property.
2. Dishonest misappropriation, conversion, or use in violation of direction.

**Punishment**:
- Section 406: Up to 10 years imprisonment OR fine OR both.
- Section 407: CBT by carrier/wharfinger — up to 15 years AND fine.
- Section 408: CBT by clerk/servant — up to 15 years AND fine.
- Section 409: CBT by public servant/agent/banker — 2–20 years AND whipping AND fine.

**Distinguished from theft**: CBT involves entrustment; theft involves taking without consent.

**Cases**: *PP v Datuk Tan Cheng Swee* [1980] 2 MLJ 277; *Periasamy s/o Sinnappan v PP* [1996] 2 MLJ 557.
topics.description: Misappropriation by person entrusted with property.

topics.title: Cheating (Sections 415–420)
topics.content:
**Section 415**: Whoever by deceiving any person:
(a) fraudulently or dishonestly induces the deceived to deliver any property, or to consent that any person shall retain property; OR
(b) intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do if not so deceived, and which causes or is likely to cause damage or harm.

**Section 417 — Punishment**: Up to 5 years imprisonment OR fine OR both.

**Section 419**: Cheating by personation — up to 7 years imprisonment OR fine OR both.

**Section 420**: Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property — 1–10 years AND whipping AND fine.

**Distinguished from CBT**: Cheating involves deception at inception; CBT involves entrustment with subsequent dishonesty.

**Cases**: *Mohamed Ali bin Jaafar v PP* [1962] MLJ 230; *Hong Chee How v PP* [2003] 4 MLJ 369.
topics.description: Deception inducing delivery of property or causing damage.

topics.title: Forgery (Sections 463–477A)
topics.content:
**Section 463**: Whoever makes any false document or part of a document with intent to cause damage or injury to the public or any person, or to support any claim or title, or to cause any person to part with property, or to enter into express or implied contract, or with intent to commit fraud or that fraud may be committed, commits forgery.

**Section 464**: When a person is said to make a false document.

**Punishments**:
- Section 465: Forgery — up to 2 years imprisonment OR fine OR both.
- Section 467: Forgery of valuable security/will — up to 20 years OR fine OR both.
- Section 468: Forgery for purpose of cheating — up to 7 years AND fine.
- Section 471: Using as genuine a forged document — same as forgery.
- Section 477A: Falsification of accounts — up to 7 years OR fine OR both.

**Cases**: *Jamali Bin Adnan v PP* [1986] 1 MLJ 162; *PP v Lim Kim Mooi* [1996] 4 MLJ 533.
topics.description: Making false documents with intent to cause damage or fraud.

topics.title: Sexual Offences (Sections 354–377E)
topics.description: Outrage of modesty, rape, incest, sexual connection by deception.

topics.title: Kidnapping, Abduction, and Trafficking
topics.content:
**Section 359**: Kidnapping is of two kinds — from Malaysia or from lawful guardianship.

**Section 360 — Kidnapping from Malaysia**: Conveying person beyond Malaysia limits without consent.
**Section 361 — From lawful guardianship**: Taking minor (under 14 male / 16 female) or person of unsound mind out of keeping of guardian without consent.
**Section 363 — Punishment**: Up to 7 years AND fine.

**Section 362 — Abduction**: By force compelling, or by deceitful means inducing, any person to go from any place.

**Section 364 — Kidnapping for murder**: Up to 30 years.
**Section 364A — Kidnapping for ransom**: Death or imprisonment for life AND whipping.
**Section 365 — For wrongful confinement**: Up to 7 years AND fine.

**Anti-Trafficking in Persons & Anti-Smuggling of Migrants Act 2007 (ATIPSOM)**: Specific offences for human trafficking; minimum 3 years up to 20 years AND fine.
topics.description: Sections 359–374 Penal Code and ATIP Act 2007.

topics.title: Dangerous Drugs Act 1952
topics.content:
**Key offences**:
- **Section 6**: Importation/exportation of dangerous drugs.
- **Section 12**: Possession of dangerous drugs (up to 5 years OR RM20,000).
- **Section 13**: Self-administration (up to 2 years OR RM5,000).
- **Section 39A(1)**: Possession of specified amounts (2–5 years AND whipping).
- **Section 39A(2)**: Aggravated possession (5 years to life AND whipping not less than 10 strokes).
- **Section 39B**: Trafficking — formerly mandatory death; since amendments 2018 & 2023, court has discretion.

**Trafficking thresholds (Section 37(da))**:
- Cannabis: 200g.
- Heroin/morphine: 15g.
- Methamphetamine: 50g.
- Cocaine: 40g.
- Ketamine: 100g.

**Statutory presumptions**:
- Section 37(d): Possession of 'custody or control' presumes knowledge.
- Section 37(da): Possession of specified amount presumes trafficking.
- Section 37(g): Premises in possession or under control of accused — presumed knowledge.
- Section 37(h): Vehicle keys.

**Burden**: Statutory presumptions rebuttable on balance of probabilities (*PP v Yuvaraj*).

**Cases**: *Muhammed bin Hassan v PP* [1998] 2 MLJ 273; *Ong Ah Chuan v PP* [1981] 1 MLJ 64.
topics.description: Trafficking, possession, presumptions, and capital sentencing.

topics.title: MACC Act 2009
topics.content:
Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission Act 2009 (Act 694) replaces Anti-Corruption Act 1997.

**Key offences**:
- **Section 16**: Soliciting/accepting/giving gratification.
- **Section 17(a)**: Officer of public body soliciting/accepting gratification.
- **Section 17(b)**: Person giving gratification to officer of public body.
- **Section 18**: Offences relating to procurements.
- **Section 21**: Bribery of officer of public body to procure contract.
- **Section 23**: Using office or position for gratification.
- **Section 25**: Failure to declare gratification.
- **Section 36**: Offence of false claim.
- **Section 17A** (since 2020): Corporate liability — commercial organisations liable for corrupt acts of associated persons; defence of adequate procedures.

**Punishment**: Up to 20 years AND fine of not less than 5x value of gratification or RM10,000 (whichever higher).

**Presumptions (Sections 50, 51, 52, 53)**: Wide presumptions in favour of prosecution; rebuttable on balance of probabilities.
topics.description: Bribery, corruption offences, and procedural framework.

topics.title: Sedition Act 1948
topics.content:
**Section 3 — Seditious tendency**:
(a) Bring into hatred or contempt or excite disaffection against any Ruler/Government.
(b) Excite subjects to attempt to procure alteration otherwise than by lawful means.
(c) Bring into hatred/contempt/disaffection against the administration of justice.
(d) Raise discontent or disaffection amongst subjects.
(e) Promote feelings of ill-will and hostility between different races or classes.
(f) Question matters protected by Part III of Constitution (citizenship), Article 152 (national language), Article 153 (Malay/Bumiputra position), Article 181 (Sovereignty of Rulers).

**Section 4 — Punishment**: First offence — fine up to RM5,000 OR imprisonment up to 3 years OR both. Second offence — up to 5 years imprisonment.

**Section 4(1A)**: If causes bodily injury or damage to property — 3–7 years imprisonment.

**Defences (Section 3(2))**: Pointing out errors in government, lawful changes, etc., done in good faith — but very limited in practice.

**Cases**: *PP v Mark Koding* [1983] 1 MLJ 111; *PP v Azmi Sharom* [2015] 8 CLJ 921.
topics.description: Sedition tendency and key offences.

topics.title: Communications and Multimedia Act 1998
topics.content:
**Section 233(1)(a)**: A person commits an offence if he, by means of any network facilities or network service or applications service, knowingly:
- makes, creates or solicits, AND
- initiates the transmission of
any comment, request, suggestion or other communication which is **obscene, indecent, false, menacing or offensive in character with intent to annoy, abuse, threaten or harass another person**.

**Section 233(3) — Punishment**: Fine up to RM50,000 OR imprisonment up to 1 year OR both, AND further fine of RM1,000 each day during which offence continues after conviction.

**Common usage**: Online statements, social media posts, emails.

**Constitutional concerns**: Tested in *PP v Rutinin Suhaimin* [2013]; *Mat Shuhaimi Shafiei v PP* [2014]. Article 10 freedom of expression considerations.

**Section 211 — Content prohibition**: Prohibits content service provider from providing offensive content.
topics.description: Section 233 — improper use of network facilities.

topics.title: Penal Code Section 124 — Activities Detrimental to Parliamentary Democracy
topics.content:
**Section 124B**: Whoever, by any means, directly or indirectly, commits an activity detrimental to parliamentary democracy — imprisonment up to 20 years.

**Section 124C**: Attempt to commit activity detrimental to parliamentary democracy — up to 15 years.

**Section 124D**: Printing, publishing, sale, etc. of documents detrimental to parliamentary democracy — up to 5 years.

**Section 124K**: Sabotage — death or imprisonment for life.

**Section 124L**: Attempt to commit sabotage — up to 30 years.

**'Activity detrimental to parliamentary democracy' (Section 130A)**: An activity carried out by a person or group of persons designed to overthrow or undermine parliamentary democracy by violent or unconstitutional means.

**Procedural**: Many of these are scheduled offences under Security Offences (Special Measures) Act 2012 (SOSMA) — special procedures for arrest, detention, and trial.
topics.description: Sections 124B, 124C, and related security offences.

topics.title: SOSMA 2012 — Security Offences (Special Measures) Act
topics.content:
**Schedule 1**: Lists offences treated as 'security offences' (Penal Code Chapter VI, VIA, terrorism offences).

**Key special provisions**:
- **Section 3**: Application — only to security offences in Schedule.
- **Section 4**: Power of arrest without warrant; detention up to 28 days for investigation (versus 14 days under CPC s.117).
- **Section 5**: Right to access legal practitioner may be delayed up to 48 hours.
- **Section 6**: Right to family communication.
- **Section 7**: Restrictions on movement after release.
- **Section 8**: Investigation by police officer not below rank of Superintendent.
- **Section 13**: Bail not granted except for woman, child, or sick person.
- **Section 14**: Trial — Sessions Court with single judge for non-capital; High Court for capital.
- **Section 30**: Special evidentiary rules — admissibility of intercepted communications.

**Sunset clause**: Reviewed every 5 years by Parliament.

**Cases**: *Mohamad Hatta Rosli v Government of Malaysia* [2017]; constitutional challenge in *PP v Khairuddin Abu Hassan* [2016].
topics.description: Special procedures for security offences.

topics.title: Anti-Money Laundering Act 2001 (AMLA)
topics.content:
**Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001 (Act 613).**

**Section 4 — Money laundering offence**: Whoever:
(a) engages in transaction involving proceeds of unlawful activity;
(b) acquires/receives/possesses/disguises/transfers/uses such proceeds;
(c) removes such proceeds from or brings into Malaysia;
(d) conceals/disguises/impedes recovery —
is liable.

**Punishment**: Imprisonment up to 15 years AND fine of not less than 5x value of proceeds OR RM5 million (whichever higher).

**Section 14**: Reporting obligation by reporting institutions (banks, lawyers, accountants) — Suspicious Transaction Reports (STR).

**Section 50–55**: Forfeiture of property — civil and criminal.

**Predicate offences (Second Schedule)**: Over 200 listed serious offences across statutes.

**Cases**: *PP v Billion Nova Sdn Bhd* [2017]; *Lim Guan Eng v PP* [2020].
topics.description: Money laundering, predicate offences, and reporting obligations.

topics.title: Domestic Violence Act 1994
topics.content:
**Definition (Section 2)**: 'Domestic violence' includes wilfully or knowingly placing victim in fear of physical injury, causing physical injury by such act known/ought to be known to result in injury, compelling acts to which victim has right to abstain, confining/detaining against will, causing mischief or destruction of property.

**Categories of victims**: Spouse, former spouse, child, incapacitated adult, any other family member.

**Interim Protection Order (Section 4)**: Issued during investigation; up to 12 months.

**Protection Order (Section 5)**: Issued after charge filed.

**Enhanced sentences**: When a Penal Code offence (e.g., causing hurt) is committed in domestic violence context, courts apply DVA in conjunction.

**Penal Code Section 326A** (added by amendment): Causing hurt to spouse — up to 10 years AND fine.

**Process**: Reports to police, Welfare Department (JKM), or directly to Magistrate.
topics.description: Protection orders and domestic violence offences.

topics.title: Evidence Act 1950 — Overview and Structure
topics.content:
The **Evidence Act 1950 (Act 56)** governs admissibility of evidence in Malaysian courts.

**Structure**:
- Part I (ss.1-55): Relevancy of facts.
- Part II (ss.56-100): Proof.
- Part III (ss.101-167): Production and effect of evidence.

**Key principles**:
- **Section 5**: Evidence may be given of facts in issue and relevant facts only.
- **Section 6**: Res gestae — facts forming part of same transaction.
- **Sections 7–11**: Occasion, cause, motive, conduct, alibi.
- **Sections 17–31**: Admissions and confessions.
- **Section 32**: Statements by deceased / unavailable persons.
- **Section 45**: Expert opinions.
- **Sections 56–58**: Judicial notice.
- **Section 60**: Oral evidence must be direct.
- **Sections 61–73**: Documentary evidence; primary and secondary evidence.
- **Section 74**: Public documents.
- **Section 90A**: Computer-produced documents.
- **Section 101**: Burden of proof; prosecution must prove case beyond reasonable doubt.
topics.description: Scheme of the Act, relevance, and admissibility.

topics.title: Confessions (Sections 24–30 EA)
topics.content:
**Section 24**: Confession is irrelevant if caused by inducement, threat, or promise from person in authority.

**Section 25**: No confession made to a police officer shall be proved against accused (subject to s.27).

**Section 26**: Confession by accused while in police custody not admissible unless made in immediate presence of Magistrate.

**Section 27**: Information leading to discovery of fact admissible — even if from accused in custody.

**Section 28**: Confession after removal of inducement.

**Section 29**: Confession otherwise relevant not irrelevant because of promise of secrecy or deception.

**Section 30**: Confession affecting co-accused jointly tried.

**Cautioned statement (Section 113 CPC)**: Statement to police after caution; admissible if voluntary. Test in *Dato' Mokhtar bin Hashim v PP* [1983] 2 MLJ 232 — voluntariness determined in trial within trial.

**Burden**: Prosecution must prove voluntariness beyond reasonable doubt.
topics.description: Cautioned statements, voluntariness, and admissibility.

topics.title: Identification Evidence
topics.content:
**Identification by witnesses** is treated with caution due to high risk of error.

**Identification parade procedure**:
1. Conducted by police officer, ideally not investigating officer.
2. Suspect placed amongst at least 8 persons of similar appearance.
3. Witness invited to point out suspect.
4. Conducted in presence of officer of rank not below Inspector.
5. Documented; defence counsel may be present.

**Turnbull Guidelines** (*R v Turnbull* [1977] QB 224, applied in *PP v Mohamad Terang Bin Amit* [1999] 1 MLJ 154):
- **A** — Amount of time under observation.
- **D** — Distance from witness.
- **V** — Visibility (lighting, obstructions).
- **O** — Obstructions to view.
- **K** — Known or seen before.
- **A** — Any reason to remember.
- **T** — Time lapse since observation.
- **E** — Errors or discrepancies in earlier description.

**Dock identification**: Generally inadmissible; identification parade preferred.

**Cases**: *Jaafar bin Ali v PP* [1998] 4 MLJ 423; *Arumugam Mothiyah v PP* [1995] 1 CLJ 58.
topics.description: Identification parades and Turnbull guidelines.

topics.title: Expert Evidence (Section 45 EA)
topics.content:
**Section 45 EA**: When the court has to form an opinion upon a point of foreign law, science or art, or as to identity or genuineness of handwriting or finger impressions, the opinions upon that point of persons specially skilled in such foreign law, science or art, or in questions as to identity, or genuineness of handwriting or finger impressions are relevant facts.

**Such persons are called experts.**

**Conditions for admissibility**:
1. Subject matter beyond common knowledge.
2. Witness has special knowledge through training, study, or experience.
3. Evidence is on a matter requiring expert opinion.

**Common areas**: Forensic medicine, DNA analysis, ballistics, handwriting, accounting, IT/digital forensics, drug analysis (chemist), valuation.

**Weight**: Court not bound by expert opinion (*Ong Chan Tow v R* [1963] MLJ 160). Court must evaluate basis, methodology, and credibility.

**Cases**: *Wong Swee Chin v PP* [1981] 1 MLJ 212; *Junaidi bin Abdullah v PP* [1993] 3 MLJ 217 — chain of custody for chemist's report.
topics.description: Admissibility, weight, and limitations of expert testimony.

topics.title: Hearsay and Exceptions
topics.content:
**General rule**: A statement made out of court is inadmissible to prove the truth of its contents.

**Statutory exceptions in Evidence Act 1950**:
- **Section 6**: Res gestae — same transaction.
- **Section 8**: Conduct, motive, preparation.
- **Section 17**: Admissions.
- **Section 32**: Statements by persons who cannot be called as witnesses (deceased, untraceable, abroad, etc.) — including dying declarations, statements in course of business, against pecuniary/proprietary interest.
- **Section 33**: Evidence given in previous proceeding.
- **Section 35**: Entries in public records.
- **Section 73A**: Documentary evidence in civil proceedings (adopted with caution in criminal).
- **Section 90A**: Computer documents — wide admissibility.

**Common law exceptions**: Spontaneous exclamations, statements accompanying acts.

**Cases**: *Subramaniam v PP* [1956] MLJ 220 — distinction between statement to prove its truth (hearsay) versus to prove its making (admissible).
topics.description: Rule against hearsay and statutory exceptions.

topics.title: Principles of Sentencing
topics.content:
**Four classical aims (PP v Loo Choon Fatt [1976] 2 MLJ 256)**:
1. **Retribution** — punishment proportionate to wrongdoing.
2. **Deterrence** — general (society) and specific (offender).
3. **Prevention** — incapacitation.
4. **Rehabilitation** — reform of offender.

**Sentencing process**:
1. Identify the offence and statutory range.
2. Assess gravity (objective seriousness).
3. Identify aggravating factors.
4. Identify mitigating factors.
5. Consider personal circumstances.
6. Apply totality principle (multiple offences).
7. Consider time spent in remand (Section 282(d) CPC — court may consider).
8. Pronounce sentence with reasons.

**Public interest**: Tan Bok Yeng v PP [1972] 1 MLJ 214 — sentence must reflect public interest, not just personal mitigation.

**Plea of guilty discount**: One-third reduction is common but not automatic — *Sau Soo Kim v PP* [1975] 2 MLJ 134.
topics.description: Aims, factors, and judicial approach to sentencing.

topics.title: Mitigating and Aggravating Factors
topics.content:
**Mitigating factors**:
- First offender (clean record).
- Plea of guilty (especially early).
- Genuine remorse / restitution to victim.
- Cooperation with authorities.
- Youth or advanced age.
- Family circumstances (sole breadwinner, dependants).
- Health (terminal illness, mental health).
- Provocation, duress, momentary lapse.
- Rehabilitation efforts (counselling, employment).
- Delay in prosecution not attributable to accused.

**Aggravating factors**:
- Premeditation, planning.
- Breach of trust (employer, fiduciary, family).
- Vulnerable victim (child, elderly, disabled).
- Position of authority abused.
- Use of weapon, violence, or threats.
- Multiple victims.
- Prevalence of the offence.
- Previous convictions (especially similar).
- Lack of remorse.
- Sophisticated commission.

**Personal mitigation in serious offences**: Limited weight where offence is grave and prevalent — *Bachik bin Abdul Rahman v PP* [2004] 2 MLJ 534.
topics.description: Personal and offence-related factors in sentencing.

topics.title: Death Penalty and Recent Reforms
topics.content:
**Abolition of Mandatory Death Penalty Act 2023 (Act 846)** (effective 4 July 2023) abolished mandatory death for:
- Section 39B Dangerous Drugs Act (trafficking).
- Section 302 Penal Code (murder).
- Section 364A (kidnapping for ransom — partially).
- Firearms Act offences.

**Judicial discretion**: Court may impose death OR imprisonment of 30–40 years AND whipping not less than 12 strokes.

**Revision of Sentence of Death and Imprisonment for Natural Life Act 2023**: Federal Court (in special panel) may review existing death sentences and natural life imprisonments imposed before the Act, replacing them with discretionary sentences.

**Considerations (Federal Court guidance)**:
- Nature and circumstances of offence.
- Manner of commission.
- Impact on victim and society.
- Rehabilitative potential.
- Mitigating factors.

**Cases**: *Pendakwa Raya v Letitia Bosman* [2023] (post-amendment landmark).
topics.description: Mandatory death abolition and judicial discretion.

topics.title: Whipping and Imprisonment
topics.content:
**Whipping (Sections 286–293 CPC, Whipping Rules 1953)**:
- Maximum 24 strokes (adult); 10 strokes (juvenile).
- Inflicted with single rotan; specifications by rules.
- Carried out in prison; medical officer present.
- Not on persons under 18 in some categories; not on women (Section 289 CPC).
- Not on males above 50 unless drug offences.
- Suspended if accused medically unfit.

**Imprisonment (Sections 282–284 CPC)**:
- **Simple imprisonment** vs **rigorous imprisonment**.
- Multiple sentences may run concurrently or consecutively (Section 282(d)).
- Time in remand may be deducted at court's discretion (Section 282(d)).
- Life imprisonment generally means imprisonment for natural life (now subject to discretionary review under 2023 Act).

**Special sentencing options**:
- **Bond for good behaviour** (Section 173A CPC) — minor offences.
- **Community service** for first offenders (limited).
- **Probation** (Probation of Offenders Act 1954).
- **Compensation** to victim (Section 426 CPC).
topics.description: Whipping under Sections 286–293 CPC and rules.

topics.title: Child Act 2001
topics.content:
**Child Act 2001 (Act 611)** governs children (under 18) in conflict with the law.

**Key principles**:
- Best interests of the child (Section 3).
- Doli incapax: no offence by child under 10 (Section 82 Penal Code); rebuttable presumption for child 10–12 (Section 83).

**Court for Children**:
- Established under Section 11.
- Comprises Magistrate and 2 advisers (one woman where practicable).
- Closed hearings; no publication of identifying information (Section 15).

**Sentencing options (Section 91)**:
(a) Admonish and discharge.
(b) Discharge on bond for good behaviour.
(c) Probation (up to 3 years).
(d) Approved school.
(e) Henry Gurney School (juvenile rehabilitation).
(f) Whipping (limited; not for girls).
(g) Fine, compensation, or costs.
(h) Imprisonment (only for those 14+ and where no alternative).

**Death sentence prohibited** for offences committed under 18 (Section 97).

**Cases**: *Loh Wai Lian v PP* [1986] 1 MLJ 67; *PP v Sambo* [1979] 1 MLJ 217.
topics.description: Children in conflict with the law.

topics.title: Sexual Offences Against Children Act 2017
topics.content:
**Sexual Offences Against Children Act 2017 (Act 792)** complements Penal Code provisions.

**Key offences**:
- Section 4: Making child pornography — up to 30 years AND not less than 6 strokes whipping.
- Section 5: Possession/access of child pornography — up to 5 years OR fine RM10,000 OR both.
- Section 6: Using child for child pornography.
- Section 7: Exchange child for sexual purposes.
- Section 8: Causing child to participate in pornographic activities.
- Section 9: Sexual communication with child — up to 3 years OR fine RM10,000 OR both.
- Section 10: Sexual assault of child.
- Section 11: Physical sexual assault on child.
- Section 12: Non-physical sexual assault.
- Section 14: Child grooming — up to 5 years OR fine RM20,000 OR both.
- Section 15: Person in relationship of trust — enhanced penalty.

**Section 17**: Offences extra-territorial — Malaysian citizens/residents committing abroad.

**Section 19**: Mandatory report by certain professionals.
topics.description: Specific protection regime for child sexual exploitation.

topics.title: Cyber Crime — CMA, Penal Code, Computer Crimes Act
topics.content:
**Computer Crimes Act 1997 (Act 563)**:
- Section 3: Unauthorised access to computer material.
- Section 4: Unauthorised access with intent to commit offence.
- Section 5: Unauthorised modification of computer contents.
- Section 6: Wrongful communication.
- Section 7: Abetments and attempts.

**Penalties**: Up to 10 years imprisonment AND/OR fines up to RM150,000.

**Communications and Multimedia Act 1998**:
- Section 233: Improper use of network facilities.
- Section 211: Offensive content.

**Penal Code (post-2017 amendments)**:
- Section 233A: Cheating using computer/electronic means.
- Various forgery and CBT provisions applied to digital contexts.

**Personal Data Protection Act 2010**: Misuse of personal data — fines and imprisonment.

**Investigation challenges**: Digital evidence, chain of custody, jurisdictional issues, encryption.

**Section 90A EA**: Computer-generated documents admissible if certificate produced.
topics.description: Legal framework for digital and cyber offences.

case_laws.summary: Federal Court restated the test for prima facie case at the close of prosecution evidence.
case_laws.case_name: PP v Mohd Radzi bin Abu Bakar
case_laws.full_text: The Federal Court redefined the prima facie test, holding that the trial court must subject prosecution evidence to maximum evaluation and call upon the accused to enter defence only if such evidence, if unrebutted, would warrant conviction.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. At close of prosecution case, court determines whether prima facie case made out.
2. Test is maximum evaluation of prosecution evidence.
3. If evidence unrebutted would warrant conviction — defence called.
4. If credible evidence is wanting on any ingredient — accused acquitted.

case_laws.summary: Federal Court clarified meaning of 'prima facie case' and 'maximum evaluation'.
case_laws.full_text: Augustine Paul FCJ delivered judgment clarifying that maximum evaluation requires the trial court to consider whether the prosecution witnesses were credible and whether their testimony, taken at its highest, established each ingredient of the offence.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Prima facie case requires credible evidence on each ingredient.
2. Maximum evaluation includes assessment of credibility.
3. Where prosecution evidence is inherently incredible, no prima facie case.
4. Court not bound to call defence where evidence unreliable.

case_laws.summary: Right to counsel under Article 5(3) — when it attaches and reasonable delay.
case_laws.case_name: Ooi Ah Phua v Officer-in-Charge Criminal Investigation, Kedah
case_laws.full_text: Suffian LP held that the right to consult and be defended by counsel under Article 5(3) attaches upon arrest, but the police may delay access where immediate consultation would prejudice investigation. The delay must be reasonable, judged on the facts of each case.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Right to consult counsel attaches upon arrest.
2. Police may delay access for reasonable time to allow investigation.
3. Reasonableness depends on facts.
4. Detained person may not be denied access altogether.

case_laws.summary: Article 5(1) read with Article 8(1) embodies substantive due process.
case_laws.full_text: Gopal Sri Ram FCJ delivered seminal judgment establishing substantive due process under Malaysian Constitution. Held that 'law' in Article 5(1) does not mean any law, but law that conforms to the Constitution and accepted norms of justice.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Word 'law' in Article 5(1) refers to substantive law incorporating principles of natural justice.
2. Constitution to be interpreted broadly and liberally.
3. Right to fair trial is a fundamental right.
4. Inherent right to silence and presumption of innocence.

case_laws.summary: Standard of proof on accused to rebut statutory presumption.
case_laws.full_text: Privy Council held that where a statute creates a presumption against the accused, the burden of rebutting it is on the balance of probabilities — a lower standard than that imposed on the prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Statutory presumption shifts burden to accused.
2. Standard for rebuttal: balance of probabilities.
3. Lower than 'beyond reasonable doubt'.
4. Authoritative on burden under Section 105 EA 1950.

case_laws.summary: Burden of proof and approach to defence evidence.
case_laws.full_text: Suffian J formulated the famous 'three-tier' test: (1) if you accept defence story, acquit; (2) if you do not accept but it raises reasonable doubt, acquit; (3) if you do not accept and it does not raise reasonable doubt, prosecution case must be examined for proof beyond reasonable doubt.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Prosecution must prove case beyond reasonable doubt.
2. Defence need only raise reasonable doubt.
3. If defence story is reasonably true, accused must be acquitted.
4. Even if defence story is improbable, if reasonably possible — acquit.

case_laws.summary: Murder — application of Exception 4 (sudden fight).
case_laws.full_text: Federal Court considered the application of Exception 4 to Section 300 — sudden fight in heat of passion. Held that all four conditions must be present: sudden quarrel, in heat of passion, without premeditation, and without taking undue advantage or acting in cruel manner.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Sudden fight requires absence of premeditation.
2. Must be in heat of passion.
3. No undue advantage taken or cruel/unusual manner used.
4. Reduces murder to culpable homicide.

case_laws.summary: Section 300(c) — bodily injury sufficient in ordinary course of nature.
case_laws.full_text: Raja Azlan Shah FJ adopted Indian Supreme Court's analysis in *Virsa Singh v State of Punjab*: intention to inflict the injury must be proved subjectively, but whether the injury is sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature is an objective inquiry.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Section 300(c) requires intention to cause that particular injury.
2. Court considers whether injury sufficient in ordinary course of nature.
3. Objective test as to sufficiency.
4. Subjective test as to intention to cause that injury.

case_laws.summary: Section 39B DDA — trafficking and double presumption rule.
case_laws.full_text: Federal Court held that the prosecution cannot rely on the presumption of possession under Section 37(d) to invoke the presumption of trafficking under Section 37(da). Possession must first be proved by direct or actual physical custody and control before the trafficking presumption arises.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Court cannot use Section 37(d) presumption to invoke Section 37(da).
2. Cannot pile presumption upon presumption.
3. Possession must be proved as fact before s.37(da) operates.
4. Or both presumptions must be invoked separately on different facts.

case_laws.summary: Mandatory death penalty under MDA — constitutionality.
case_laws.full_text: Privy Council upheld constitutionality of mandatory death penalty in Singapore's Misuse of Drugs Act (similar to Malaysian DDA). The judgment was followed in Malaysia for decades but its practical effect has been displaced by the Abolition of Mandatory Death Penalty Act 2023.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Mandatory death penalty for trafficking is constitutional.
2. Differential treatment based on quantity is rational.
3. Quantity threshold a legitimate legislative classification.
4. Long-influential authority — though now subject to 2023 reforms abolishing mandatory death.

case_laws.summary: Charge framing — particulars and notice to accused.
case_laws.full_text: Court emphasised that the purpose of a charge is to give the accused notice of the matter he is accused of, so he may prepare his defence. Defects which do not occasion a failure of justice may be cured.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Charge must give accused fair notice of allegation.
2. Particulars of time, place, and manner essential.
3. Defective charge may be cured if no prejudice (Section 422).
4. Failure of justice test.

case_laws.summary: Chemist's report — chain of custody and admissibility.
case_laws.full_text: Supreme Court held that in drug cases the prosecution must prove a complete and unbroken chain of custody from seizure to chemist's analysis. Any gap in the chain raises reasonable doubt as to whether the substance analysed was the substance seized from the accused.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Prosecution must prove unbroken chain of custody.
2. Specimen examined must be the one seized.
3. Failure breaks chain — fatal to prosecution.
4. Each handler must testify or be accounted for.

case_laws.summary: Hearsay rule — when out-of-court statement admissible.
case_laws.full_text: Privy Council held that statements made by terrorists to the accused (claimed under duress) were admissible not to prove what the terrorists said was true, but to prove the effect on the accused's mind in raising the defence of duress.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Statement is hearsay if tendered to prove truth of contents.
2. Statement is original evidence (not hearsay) if tendered to prove its making or its effect on hearer.
3. Distinction is the purpose of tendering.
4. Foundational case on hearsay rule.

case_laws.summary: Classical exposition of sentencing principles in Malaysia.
case_laws.full_text: Hashim Yeop A Sani J set out the four classical aims of sentencing — retribution, deterrence, prevention, and rehabilitation — and emphasized that the court must balance these aims with the personal circumstances of the offender.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Aims of punishment: retribution, deterrence, prevention, rehabilitation.
2. Court must balance public interest against personal mitigation.
3. Sentence must reflect seriousness of offence.
4. Sentencing not a mathematical exercise.

case_laws.summary: Personal mitigation in serious offences carries limited weight.
case_laws.case_name: Bachik bin Abdul Rahman v PP
case_laws.full_text: Court of Appeal held that in offences involving public safety or prevalent crimes, personal mitigation such as first offender status or family circumstances, while relevant, must yield to the overriding public interest in deterrent sentencing.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Personal circumstances yield to public interest in serious offences.
2. Prevalence of offence is aggravating factor.
3. Deterrence is paramount in some cases.
4. Mitigation cannot reduce sentence below proportionate level.

case_laws.summary: Right to counsel during remand under Article 5(3).
case_laws.case_name: Hashim bin Saud v Yahaya bin Hashim
case_laws.full_text: Federal Court held that the right to consult counsel under Article 5(3) extends to a person under remand. The police's discretion to delay access must be exercised reasonably and access cannot be indefinitely refused.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Right to counsel applies during remand.
2. Police cannot indefinitely deny access.
3. Magistrate must ensure access on application.
4. Confessions obtained without counsel may be inadmissible.

case_laws.summary: Criminal Breach of Trust by public servant — Section 409.
case_laws.full_text: Federal Court analysed the elements of CBT under Section 409 and emphasised that breach of trust by public servants strikes at the foundation of public administration, warranting deterrent sentencing.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. CBT requires entrustment plus dishonest misappropriation.
2. Public servant CBT carries enhanced penalty.
3. Fiduciary position relevant to sentencing.
4. Restitution does not erase criminal liability.

case_laws.summary: Voluntariness of cautioned statements — trial within trial.
case_laws.case_name: Dato' Mokhtar bin Hashim v PP
case_laws.full_text: Federal Court laid down the procedure for determining the voluntariness of cautioned statements via trial within trial. The prosecution bears the burden of proving voluntariness beyond reasonable doubt before the statement can be admitted.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Voluntariness must be proved by prosecution beyond reasonable doubt.
2. Trial within trial determines admissibility.
3. Threats, inducements, oppression render statement inadmissible.
4. Court considers totality of circumstances.

case_laws.summary: Common intention — Section 34 — formation may be on the spot.
case_laws.full_text: Supreme Court clarified that common intention under Section 34 need not be pre-meditated and may form spontaneously, but a meeting of minds and shared purpose must be inferred from the surrounding circumstances.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Common intention may be pre-arranged or formed on the spot.
2. Mere participation insufficient — meeting of minds required.
3. Inferred from conduct, presence, and circumstances.
4. Each participant liable for collective act.

case_laws.summary: Common intention vs common object distinction.
case_laws.full_text: Supreme Court analysed the interplay between Sections 34 and 149, emphasising that while Section 34 requires actual participation, Section 149 makes mere membership of an unlawful assembly with common object sufficient for liability.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Section 34 requires participation in criminal act.
2. Section 149 imputes liability by membership of unlawful assembly.
3. Section 34 narrower; Section 149 wider liability.
4. Both may apply to same facts.

case_laws.summary: Constitutionality of Sedition Act under Article 10 freedom of speech.
case_laws.full_text: Federal Court upheld the constitutionality of the Sedition Act, holding that restrictions on freedom of speech under Article 10(2)(a) are valid where Parliament has determined them necessary in interests of security or public order.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Sedition Act is valid law under Article 10(2)(a).
2. Restrictions on speech must be reasonable and proportionate.
3. Court will not strike down legislation unless clearly unconstitutional.
4. Pre-Merdeka law preserved by Article 162.

case_laws.summary: Section 117 CPC remand — limits and judicial review.
case_laws.full_text: High Court emphasised that Section 117 CPC requires Magistrates to exercise independent judicial discretion and not merely endorse police requests for remand. Reasons must be recorded and the duration tailored to investigation needs.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Magistrate must independently assess remand application.
2. Cannot rubber-stamp police request.
3. Reasons must be recorded.
4. Total remand cannot exceed 15 days under CPC.

case_laws.summary: Application of Abolition of Mandatory Death Penalty Act 2023.
case_laws.full_text: Federal Court applied the post-2023 sentencing framework, sentencing the accused to imprisonment instead of death after consideration of mitigating circumstances. Marks a paradigm shift from mandatory capital punishment.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Court has discretion between death and 30–40 years.
2. Considers nature of offence, manner, mitigation.
3. Death reserved for worst cases.
4. Mitigation now meaningful in capital cases.

case_laws.summary: Expert evidence — court's evaluation and weight.
case_laws.full_text: Federal Court reaffirmed that while expert evidence under Section 45 EA is admissible to assist the court on technical matters, the court remains the final arbiter and must evaluate the expert's methodology, qualifications, and reasoning.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Expert evidence is opinion, not fact.
2. Court must evaluate basis and methodology.
3. Court not bound to accept expert opinion.
4. Where two experts disagree, court considers reasoning.

case_laws.summary: Article 5(3) — meaning of 'as soon as may be'.
case_laws.case_name: Lee Mau Seng v Minister for Home Affairs
case_laws.full_text: Wee Chong Jin CJ held that 'as soon as may be' in Article 5(3) does not mean immediately, but does mean without any unreasonable delay. The reasonableness depends on the circumstances of each case.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. 'As soon as may be' means without unreasonable delay.
2. What is reasonable is fact-dependent.
3. Police duty to facilitate access to counsel.
4. Persuasive authority in Malaysia.

case_laws.summary: Sedition Act — questioning constitutional rights of races.
case_laws.full_text: Federal Court convicted the accused (a Member of Parliament) for sedition for parliamentary speech questioning matters protected under Articles 152 and 153, holding parliamentary privilege did not immunise sedition.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Section 3(1)(f) prohibits questioning rights protected by Constitution.
2. Includes Article 152 (national language) and 153 (Malay/Bumiputra position).
3. Defences in s.3(2) limited.
4. Strict liability — no need for seditious intent.

case_laws.summary: Discount for plea of guilty.
case_laws.full_text: Federal Court endorsed the principle that an accused who pleads guilty saves court time and indicates remorse, and is therefore entitled to a discount in sentence — typically one-third — though the court retains discretion based on circumstances.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Plea of guilty entitles accused to discount.
2. One-third reduction commonly applied.
3. Not automatic — depends on circumstances.
4. Early plea attracts greater discount.

case_laws.summary: Distinction between murder and culpable homicide.
case_laws.full_text: Court of Appeal explained the relationship between Sections 299 and 300 of the Penal Code, noting that the difference is one of degree of mens rea and the presence/absence of statutory exceptions.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Murder is aggravated culpable homicide.
2. All murder is culpable homicide; not all culpable homicide is murder.
3. Difference lies in degree of intention/knowledge.
4. Exceptions reduce murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

case_laws.summary: Identification — application of Turnbull guidelines.
case_laws.full_text: Federal Court emphasised the necessity of trial judges applying the Turnbull guidelines when assessing identification evidence, particularly where conviction depends substantially on visual identification by one witness.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Trial judge must apply Turnbull guidelines.
2. Quality of identification must be assessed.
3. Single witness identification requires careful warning.
4. Conviction unsafe where guidelines not properly applied.

case_laws.summary: Reasonable doubt and circumstantial evidence.
case_laws.case_name: Pendakwa Raya v Hanif Basree Abdul Rahman
case_laws.full_text: Federal Court restated principles for circumstantial evidence — the chain of circumstances must be so complete as to admit of no other rational conclusion than the guilt of the accused, leaving no room for reasonable doubt.
case_laws.key_principles:
1. Circumstantial evidence must form unbroken chain.
2. Must point irresistibly to guilt.
3. Inconsistent with any other rational hypothesis.
4. Reasonable doubt must be based on reason.

RULES OF A VALID CHARGE (ss.152–156 CPC):
 • s.152(1): the charge must state the offence with which the accused is charged.
 • s.152(2)-(3): the offence may be described by its specific name; otherwise
   enough of the definition must be stated to give the accused notice.
 • s.152(4): the law AND the section of the law against which the offence is
   said to have been committed must be stated.
 • s.152(6): the charge must be in the language of the Court.
 • s.153: particulars as to the time and place of the alleged offence, and the
   person (if any) against whom it was committed, must be stated.
 • s.154: where the nature of the case requires it, the manner in which the
   offence was committed must be stated to give the accused notice of the
   matter charged.
 • s.156: an error or omission in the charge is not material unless the accused
   was in fact misled and a failure of justice was occasioned (read with s.422
   CPC — curable irregularity). See FAN YEW TENG v PP on the duty to frame a
   charge that conveys the precise accusation.

A. UJIAN UNDANG-UNDANG
1. Di penutup kes Pendakwaan, Mahkamah mesti menjalankan PENILAIAN MAKSIMUM
   (maximum evaluation) terhadap keterangan dan bertanya: jika saya memanggil
   OKT membela diri dan beliau berdiam diri, adakah saya sanggup mensabitkan
   atas keterangan setakat ini? Jika tidak, prima facie tidak terbukti dan OKT
   mesti dilepas dan dibebaskan: LOOI KOW CHAI v PP [2003] 2 MLJ 65 (CA);
   BALACHANDRAN v PP [2005] 2 MLJ 301 (FC); PP v MOHD RADZI bin ABU BAKAR
   [2005] 6 MLJ 393 (FC).
2. Kes prima facie ialah kes yang, jika tidak disangkal, mencukupi untuk

     seperti diterima pakai dalam JAAFAR bin ALI v PP / DATO' MOKHTAR HASHIM;
   • Rantaian keterangan (chain of evidence) terputus pada [____];
   • Percanggahan material antara saksi-saksi pada [____];
   • Tiada keterangan langsung terhadap inti pati [____].

   pertuduhan kerana Pendakwaan gagal membuktikan kes prima facie.

and concentrate fire on the weakest essential element (usually mens rea,
possession/knowledge, or identification). Quote the maximum-evaluation passage
verbatim. Even if the submission fails, it locks the prosecution's case and
frames your defence and any appeal.

cause_papers.description: Application to challenge a cautioned statement / confession as involuntary, with the s.24 Evidence Act test and the voir dire procedure (Francis Antonysamy; PP v Law Say Seck).
cause_papers.template_content:
DALAM MAHKAMAH [SESYEN / TINGGI] DI [TEMPAT]
KES JENAYAH NO: [____________]

PENDAKWA RAYA  lawan  [NAMA OKT]

──  BANTAHAN KEBOLEHTERIMAAN PENGAKUAN / PERCAKAPAN BERAMARAN  ──
(Permohonan untuk perbicaraan dalam perbicaraan — voir dire)

1. Apabila Pendakwaan cuba mengemukakan percakapan beraman / pengakuan OKT,
   pembelaan MEMBANTAH kebolehterimaannya dan memohon perbicaraan dalam
   perbicaraan (voir dire) untuk menentukan kesukarelaan.

2. UJIAN: Suatu pengakuan tidak boleh diterima jika ia dibuat akibat
   dorongan, ancaman atau janji (inducement, threat or promise) daripada
   seseorang yang berkuasa — s.24 Akta Keterangan 1950. Beban membuktikan
   kesukarelaan tanpa keraguan munasabah terletak pada PENDAKWAAN:
   FRANCIS ANTONYSAMY v PP [2005] 3 MLJ 389 (FC); PP v LAW SAY SECK;
   LEMANIT v PP.

3. ALASAN KETIDAKSUKARELAAN (worked grounds):
   (a) OKT didera / diugut secara fizikal atau psikologi semasa siasatan;
   (b) OKT dijanjikan akan dilepaskan / dibantu jika mengaku;
   (c) OKT tidak diberi amaran sewajarnya / tidak faham bahasa amaran;
   (d) OKT dinafikan akses kepada peguam, makanan, rehat atau rawatan;
   (e) Tempoh soal siasat yang berpanjangan dan menindas (oppressive).

4. PROSEDUR: Mahkamah hendaklah menangguh isu kebolehterimaan, mendengar
   keterangan kedua-dua pihak DALAM voir dire (termasuk OKT jika beliau pilih),
   dan memutuskan kesukarelaan SEBELUM kandungan pengakuan didedahkan kepada
   tribunal fakta.

OKT memohon perintah bahawa pengakuan/percakapan tersebut tidak boleh diterima
sebagai keterangan.

Bertarikh pada [tarikh].
............................................
Peguamcara bagi pihak OKT

———————————————————————————————————————————————
NOTA AMALAN: Raise the objection the moment the IO is asked to produce the
statement — do not let the contents slip in. Put each allegation of
oppression squarely to the recording officer and IO. Even if admitted,
involuntariness goes to WEIGHT and is preserved for submission and appeal.
Watch the s.27 "information leading to discovery" exception — only the part
that distinctly relates to the fact discovered is admissible.

cause_papers.title: Application to Impeach Credit of Witness (ss.145 & 155 EA)
cause_papers.description: Procedure to impeach a prosecution witness on a material contradiction with a former statement (Muthusamy v PP; Dato' Mokhtar Hashim), with the four-step Muthusamy approach.
cause_papers.template_content:
DALAM MAHKAMAH [SESYEN / TINGGI] DI [TEMPAT]
KES JENAYAH NO: [____________]

PENDAKWA RAYA  lawan  [NAMA OKT]

──  PERMOHONAN MENCABAR KREDIBILITI SAKSI (IMPEACHMENT)  ──
(Seksyen 145 & 155(c) Akta Keterangan 1950)

1. Pembelaan memohon untuk mencabar kredit saksi [nama, SP__] atas percanggahan
   material antara keterangannya di Mahkamah dan pernyataan terdahulunya
   (s.112 CPC / polis) bertarikh [____].

2. PERCANGGAHAN MATERIAL:
   • Di Mahkamah saksi berkata: "[____]".
   • Dalam pernyataan terdahulu saksi berkata: "[____]".
   Percanggahan ini menyentuh [inti pati / pengenalan / urutan kejadian] dan
   bukan remeh.

3. PROSEDUR (MUTHUSAMY v PP [1948] MLJ 57; DATO' MOKHTAR HASHIM v PP):
   (a) tunjuk percanggahan kepada saksi dan beri peluang menjelaskan;
   (b) jika penjelasan tidak memuaskan, pohon tanda pernyataan terdahulu;
   (c) Mahkamah menimbang sama ada percanggahan adalah material; dan
   (d) jika ya, Mahkamah boleh membenarkan impeachment — keseluruhan
       keterangan saksi itu kemudian dinilai dengan berhati-hati.

4. Kesan impeachment bukan automatik menolak semua keterangan saksi; ia
   memerlukan penilaian semula kredibiliti keseluruhan saksi tersebut.

Bertarikh pada [tarikh].
............................................
Peguamcara bagi pihak OKT

———————————————————————————————————————————————
NOTA AMALAN: Secure the prior statement first (via s.51A / s.112). Lay the
contradiction precisely — judges refuse impeachment for trivial discrepancies.
Always put the former statement to the witness before tendering it; springing
it without warning breaches s.145.

[Peguamcara / Timbalan Pendakwa Raya]

NOTA AMALAN: Frame recall as serving the court's search for truth, not as
filling a gap you should have closed. Identify precisely the new matter and why
it could not have been dealt with earlier.

cause_papers.title: Plea in Mitigation — Comprehensive Model (Rayuan Mitigasi)
cause_papers.description: Full worked mitigation deploying the leading sentencing authorities (Sau Soo Kim discount; Mohamed Abdullah Ang public interest; Raja Izzuddin Shah totality; Bhandulananda restraint) with model paragraphs.
cause_papers.template_content:
DALAM MAHKAMAH [____] DI [TEMPAT]
KES JENAYAH NO: [____________]

PENDAKWA RAYA  lawan  [NAMA OKT]

────────────────  RAYUAN MITIGASI  ────────────────

Yang Arif,

Saya bagi pihak OKT dengan hormatnya memohon hukuman yang setimpal dan
seadil-adilnya, dengan mengambil kira faktor-faktor berikut.

A. PRINSIP MENGIMBANGI (the sentencing balance)
   Hukuman mesti mengimbangi kepentingan awam dengan keadaan peribadi OKT:
   PP v LOO CHOON FATT [1976] 2 MLJ 256; MOHAMED ABDULLAH ANG SWEE KANG v PP
   [1988] 1 MLJ 167. Mahkamah tidak menghukum dengan dendam.

B. PENGAKUAN BERSALAH (guilty plea — the discount)
   OKT mengaku salah pada peringkat paling awal, menjimatkan masa dan kos
   Mahkamah serta saksi. Diskaun lazim satu pertiga (1/3) wajar diberi:
   SAU SOO KIM v PP [1975] 2 MLJ 134; MELVANI v PP. Pengakuan awal juga
   menunjukkan penyesalan tulen.

C. PESALAH PERTAMA & WATAK BAIK
   OKT pesalah pertama tanpa rekod lampau, berumur [__] tahun, [pekerjaan],
   menanggung [bilangan] tanggungan. Surat-surat watak dilampirkan. Peluang
   pemulihan wajar diutamakan bagi pesalah pertama: TUKIRAN bin TAIB / NEW TUCK
   SHEN v PP [1982] 1 MLJ 38.

D. FAKTOR PERIBADI & MITIGASI
   • Penyesalan dan permohonan maaf kepada mangsa;
   • Pampasan / restitusi sebanyak RM[____] telah dibayar (resit dilampirkan);
   • Kerjasama penuh dengan penyiasat;
   • Keadaan kesihatan / keluarga: [____];
   • Peranan kecil/periferi OKT dalam kejadian: [____].

E. PRINSIP KESELURUHAN (totality) & KESETARAAN (parity)
   Jika berbilang pertuduhan, jumlah hukuman keseluruhan mesti tidak melampau:
   RAJA IZZUDDIN SHAH v PP [1979] 1 MLJ 270. Hukuman OKT juga harus setara
   dengan rakan sejenayah yang dihukum [____].

F. PERMOHONAN
   OKT dengan hormatnya memohon hukuman minimum yang dibenarkan undang-undang,
   dan jika wajar, [hukuman percubaan (Bon Akhlak s.294 CPC) / perintah khidmat
   masyarakat / kompaun / penjara minimum] memandangkan rayuan campur tangan
   appellate hanya wajar jika hukuman jelas keterlaluan: BHANDULANANDA
   JAYATILAKE v PP [1982] 1 MLJ 83.

Bertarikh pada [tarikh].
............................................
Peguamcara bagi pihak OKT

———————————————————————————————————————————————
NOTA AMALAN: Lead with the strongest mitigating fact, not a recital of
biography. Tender documents (pay slips, medical reports, character letters,
restitution receipts) — assertions from the bar table carry little weight.
Where a mandatory minimum or mandatory whipping applies, address it head-on
(age >50 or female exempt from whipping: s.289 CPC).

cause_papers.title: SOSMA: Representation Against Detention & Bail Position (Act 747)
cause_papers.description: Security Offences (Special Measures) Act 2012 — the special detention regime (s.4), the no-bail rule and its exceptions (s.13), and a worked representation seeking release / electronic-tagging bail for an eligible accused.
cause_papers.template_content:
DALAM MAHKAMAH [SESYEN / TINGGI] DI [TEMPAT]
KES JENAYAH NO: [____________]

PENDAKWA RAYA  lawan  [NAMA OKT]

──  HUJAHAN / REPRESENTASI DI BAWAH AKTA KESALAHAN KESELAMATAN
    (LANGKAH-LANGKAH KHAS) 2012 ("SOSMA")  ──

1. PEMAKAIAN: SOSMA terpakai kepada "kesalahan keselamatan" yang disenaraikan
   dalam Jadual Pertama (a.l. Bab VI & VIA Kanun Keseksaan). Sahkan dahulu
   bahawa pertuduhan benar-benar suatu kesalahan keselamatan; jika tidak,
   tatacara biasa CPC terpakai.

2. PENAHANAN (s.4 SOSMA): Polis boleh menahan sehingga 28 hari bagi tujuan
   siasatan. Pembelaan hendaklah memastikan:
   (a) notis penahanan dikeluarkan dan keluarga dimaklumkan (s.4(2));
   (b) akses kepada peguam tidak dilewatkan melebihi yang dibenarkan; dan
   (c) tiada penderaan semasa tahanan.

3. JAMINAN (s.13 SOSMA): Sebagai peraturan am, seseorang yang dipertuduh dengan
   kesalahan keselamatan TIDAK boleh dijamin. PENGECUALIAN: kanak-kanak,
   wanita, dan orang yang sakit atau lemah (s.13(2)) boleh dijamin tertakluk
   kepada pemantauan elektronik (electronic monitoring device).

4. REPRESENTASI (worked):
   OKT termasuk dalam pengecualian s.13(2) kerana [wanita / berumur [__] /
   pesakit dengan laporan perubatan dilampirkan]. OKT memohon dibebaskan dengan
   jaminan tertakluk kepada peranti pemantauan elektronik dan syarat-syarat
   yang munasabah. Sebagai alternatif, jika SOSMA tidak terpakai kepada
   pertuduhan ini, OKT memohon prinsip jaminan biasa di bawah s.388 CPC.

5. NOTA: Seksyen 30 SOSMA — seseorang yang dibebaskan tetap dalam tahanan
   sehingga tempoh rayuan tamat jika Pendakwaan memberi notis rayuan; pertimbang
   implikasi ini dalam strategi.

Bertarikh pada [tarikh].
............................................
Peguamcara bagi pihak OKT

———————————————————————————————————————————————
NOTA AMALAN: First contest whether SOSMA even applies — mis-classification is a
real and reviewable issue. If the accused falls within s.13(2), build the bail
case around the exception and accept tagging. Challenge any procedural
non-compliance under s.4 (notice, access, treatment) on the record.
